title: The Dream of Homeownership Is Haunted by Eviction in This Debut Novel
desc: The premise of Andrea Uptmor’s debut novel, The New People, is both gloriously simple and fraught with tension. Newlyweds Emma and Rachel move into a recently foreclosed house in a Midwestern campus t...
content:
The premise of Andrea Uptmor’s debut novel, The New People, is both gloriously simple and fraught with tension. Newlyweds Emma and Rachel move into a recently foreclosed house in a Midwestern campus town in 2008, but unbeknownst to them, the evicted former owners Charlotte and Dirk are still living in the attic in a form of illicit cohabitation known as phrogging. The contested space of the house—which Charlotte begins to sabotage in the hopes that “the new people” will leave—ultimately grounds the novel’s larger questions about the domestic infrastructure of marriage, homeownership, and parenthood, especially for people whose access to those social institutions has been restricted.  

As a queer millennial who experienced the travails of trying to secure the legal protections of marriage well before the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges ruling, I had no idea how much it would mean to me to encounter a story like this one. Uptmor’s insights into the pressures that both legal and social queerphobia exert on Emma and Rachel’s marriage is pitch-perfect, and I loved the unexpected way in which she intertwines their struggles with those of the much older straight couple. Her approach feels refreshingly nuanced and true to the lived complexities of navigating queer adulthood in a predominantly conservative community. The book frequently made me laugh, and even moved me to tears in public. I should also mention that it is built far more sturdily than the fictional house in question, with well-finished prose and an elegantly constructed plot. In short, it’s a novel I will be thrusting into the hands of queer and straight friends alike in the coming months.

In anticipation of the book’s release, Uptmor and I had a delightful conversation over Zoom this spring about living hauntings and contested domestic spaces, as well as the intersections of queer and economic issues that drew her to revisit 2008 with these particular characters.

Jules Fitz Gerald: I once heard Carmen Maria Machado speak about all stories being haunted house stories, in the sense that they’re haunted both by their writers and by their readers. If you think of yourself as a ghost, what prompted you to haunt this particular fictional house in Indiana?



(Aşağıdaki metin orijinal dilindedir. Söyleşinin tamamına kaynak siteden ulaşabilirsiniz.)

Andrea Uptmor: This idea of illegally occupying somebody’s home has always been interesting to me. When my wife and I bought our first house in 2013 in South Minneapolis, it was in the middle of a huge rash of foreclosures in the neighborhood, and the day after we moved in, our neighbor was evicted due to foreclosure. Right after he left, a group of squatters moved in and occupied the house. Law enforcement was there all the time with their guns drawn, the windows were broken in, but they couldn’t get these people to leave. It was so fascinating to me, this idea that, for me, home ownership was about a mortgage, and for the people next door, it was about occupying a space. It wasn’t until I learned about phrogging, which is living in somebody’s house without their knowledge—sort of an actual living haunting—that I thought, oh, that’s the story. Because then you’ve got that automatic tension between the people who believe they own the house and the people who are occupying it. 

The house becomes this microcosm of what’s happening in the country.

In terms of why Indiana, that’s a good question. I was living in Iowa at the time that I wrote this and was really feeling what Emma feels throughout the book—not quite belonging, being a woman married to a woman. Like Iowa, Indiana can be one of those on-the-fence places where you just never know, when someone’s cleaning your teeth at the dentist’s office, or giving you an Uber ride, whether they’re a safe person or not. I wanted to recreate that environment for Emma and [the] other characters where there’s this air of uncertainty, where you’re not always sure if people are being intentionally aggressive or bigoted or homophobic, or whether it’s being perceived through Emma’s conditioning. 

JFG: I loved how you handled that in the book. I live very far from Indiana, in rural Oregon, but what you’re describing really resonates. Beyond the place, it was interesting as a reader to look back on that time period, especially as rights that once seemed like legal certainties–like marriage equality–are increasingly in question. What was it like for you to write 2008 from the vantage point of the present? 

AU: I’m very nostalgic for 2008. I would love to go back right now and have eight years of Obama ahead of me. But it was a pretty grim time, economically speaking. Nearly 2.5 million homeowners lost their homes to foreclosure. There was high unemployment. People’s 401Ks were tanking. There was a huge recession. At the same time, there was this brief window in California where same sex marriage was legal . . . then Proposition Eight passed, and it was no longer legal. We look back on 2008 with this sense of nostalgia and hope now, but when you were living it in the moment, people were losing their jobs, their money, their marriages, their rights to marry. It felt like the domestic infrastructure of people’s lives was disappearing. And if I wanted to write a story where a post-retirement couple was willing to endure the discomfort and humiliation of phrogging in their own attic, 2008 is probably the most likely time that this could have actually happened. The house becomes this microcosm of what’s happening in the country. The people in the attic, Charlotte and Dirk, are dealing with money issues and with a child who [lives with] addiction and mental illness. And the people downstairs, Emma and Rachel, are navigating being a queer couple in a conservative area. They’re all in the same space, but they’re having these wildly different experiences. Yet when they’re placed together in a narrative, there’s a lot of overlap. 

JFG: I really appreciated how the book is a portrait of these two different marriages at very different life stages. What led you to write Charlotte and Emma as dual narrators rather than, say, going back and forth between Emma and Rachel? 

Quite a bit of the loss [in the book] is characters having to reconcile themselves to their lives going a different way than they’d expected.

AU: It’s fun to reflect on these things because a lot of times the writing is instinctive, or you just pick up a trail. Of the four main characters, if I was going to dedicate a couple years of my life to really thinking about them, Emma and Charlotte are the two I liked the most and wanted to spend the most time with. I started with Emma because her experience most closely aligns with mine, and I think that’s often a place where writers start. I had this idea in my head, like you said, of a portrait of these two marriages, but I originally thought of them as political or generational foils, where we’ve got the conservative folks in the attic, and the lesbians downstairs, and you know, what’s gonna happen? The nuance grew through the editing. As I wrote, I realized Charlotte is so much more complex than I had originally intended, and it’s reductionist to try to just boil her down. She’s obviously Republican, but that’s not really important to the story. 

JFG: Yeah, I think of her as a secondary protagonist. 

AU: Well, she’s the one who’s got more of an agenda. Like she’s got a drive. Dirk is a little bit of her opposite in that he’s willing to just wait for things to happen. In the first draft, though, Charlotte was a lot less active. I think naturally a character who spends most of a book in an attic becomes very self-reflective. She had a lot of internalized sequences, whereas Emma is out in the world, she’s going to work, she’s going to the clinic, she’s interacting with and meeting new people, and it’s hard to balance two protagonists who are energetically very different. So in revision, Charlotte grew more into a person who is driving the story on a certain level, and she’s actually making things happen. I hate it when writers say this, but it kind of surprised me as I was writing. If we’re going to pull one spouse from each pair, they are the two most tortured. And if I’m going to read a book or write a character, I’m really interested in the tortured ones, the ones who are suffering and who are contemplating what to do about it. 

JFG: Same. I have to ask, too, with all literary allusions—like that delightful running joke between Emma and Rachel about having a Mrs. Dalloway day—who were the other books and authors lurking in the attic of your brain while you were writing? 

AU: I think the writer who has probably influenced me the most and whom I adore the most is Tessa Hadley. I always tell people I would pay money to read Tessa Hadley’s grocery list. There’s just magic in the sentences. One thing that I admire about her and have picked up from her is her ability to layer psychology on the physical world, to blur the mental landscape with the physical landscape. There are parts of The New People where I can totally tell that I was reading a Tessa Hadley novel while I was writing, and I was trying so damn hard to sound like her. You should never do that because you’ll never—she’s that category of one. 

Someone else I really love is Megha Majumdar, who wrote A Burning and A Guardian and a Thief. She writes these big stories where society is looming and impacting what’s happening on a level between two people. And yet the stories are so efficient. These are short novels that have these big, big worlds with huge consequences. She’s not afraid of a sad ending though, and I am—I can’t do it. 

JFG: I’ll resist commenting on the ending of The New People, except to say that something I love so much about Emma is how her actions keep escalating. There’s this sense of watching the train wreck happening. I also really enjoyed that she’s a writer. It’s poignant that one of the big imbalances in her marriage with Rachel is that Emma has been writing this beautiful, quiet literary novel, trying to sell it for years, and then Rachel writes this bestselling science fiction novel. What was it like to write a character who is also a writer? 

The novel is a perfect art form for shining a light on how these big systems that govern our lives, respond to something stressful.

AU: My agent would keep putting comments that said, “This is too inside baseball.” I have an MFA, which is really just a couple of years where you’re allowed to talk about writing 24 hours a day with people and you don’t have to excuse yourself. I still find it so fascinating and so interesting. Emma’s a writer, but she’s also dealing with something that a lot of creatives deal with, which is failure, this idea that when you’re creating a piece of art or a novel, most of the time, nobody has asked for it. That’s how I felt while I was writing this novel and kind of torturing myself over it like, is this going to be anything? Is this worth all the time and the tears? Nobody asked me to write this book and the world would be the same if I did or didn’t, and artists have to grapple with that all the time. Why do I keep going? What fuels me creatively? This is something that Emma doesn’t address directly because she spends so much time trying to look at anything but this creative failure. But it ties in with the rest of the book in the sense that everybody’s got some kind of invisible hope that’s dangling in front of them that keeps them going, that makes them want to want to get out of bed in the morning, and for a lot of creatives, the work is that. 

JFG: There’s a lot of loss in the book, but quite a bit of that loss is more of characters having to reconcile themselves to their lives going in a different way—or motherhood looking a different way and marriage looking a different way—from what they’d hoped or expected. I know you were just talking about hope and the more sunny side of things, but I’m fascinated by your choice to make the house itself a compromised, dangerous space at a very literal level, with the shortcuts that were taken when the house was flipped and Charlotte’s later attempts at sabotage to try to get Emma and Rachel to leave. Am I reading too much into the metaphor to think of this as an interrogation of these domestic institutions or traditional frameworks around marriage and motherhood? 

Eva Rosen recommends non-fiction about how social disparity is tied to where we live

AU: I think in some ways big metaphors and big acts of symbolism in novels are the invention of the critics. I think the writer’s job is to bring up an implausible scenario and then create an authentic setting and authentic characters around it, so that what comes out is not symbolic but the natural human output of a society. So I appreciate that reading very much. The house failing on a structural level certainly was a critique of the way that the housing market crash happened in 2008. There was such a rush to get all these houses out. There were so many predatory lenders, and so many people who did not understand what they were signing up for. And that was the point. And obviously the people who flipped Rachel and Emma’s home can stand in for all the big bad players during that time. People did not have your security or your safety in mind when all of this was happening. It was just about lining people’s pockets. 

I think the novel—not this novel in particular, but the novel in general—is a perfect art form for shining a light on how these big systems that govern our lives, the economy and political weather and the legal systems, how that plays out on a day-to-day level between two people who are talking, how they respond to something stressful. So I wouldn’t think of it naturally as symbolism, though a reader is definitely invited to think of it that way. That’s the great thing about the relationship between the writer and the reader, back to this question of haunting, is that the writer’s job is to build the house, and then move out, just get the hell out, and the reader comes in and the reader changes the lighting and moves in furniture, and that’s the most beautiful part of this whole process.

title: Migration Touches Every Life
desc: Valeria Luiselli is no stranger to incorporating tangible records of the world in her writing. In The Story of My Teeth, she exchanged audio recordings with a group of Grupo Jumex workers at a juice f...
content:
Valeria Luiselli is no stranger to incorporating tangible records of the world in her writing. In The Story of My Teeth, she exchanged audio recordings with a group of Grupo Jumex workers at a juice factory in Mexico. In Tell Me How It Ends, she listened to, transcribed, and interpreted the testimonies of undocumented children. In Lost Children Archive, the protagonist is a sound documentarist. In Echoes from the Borderlands, Luiselli moved beyond the page to bring the US-Mexico border to life in a 24-hour sonic essay/chapbook that was originally presented as a sound installation. Her newest novel, Beginning Middle End, is written in fragments and includes the sounds of volcanoes exhaling and fishermen singing, among other recordings from Sicily accessible via a QR code in the book.

Beginning Middle End is a mother-daughter road novel that journeys through time and genre. The story unfolds in vignettes as an unnamed narrator and her 12-year-old daughter travel to Sicily to return an archeological relic that the mother’s grandmother had taken years before when she migrated to Mexico. Interspersed polaroid pictures, postcards, and sounds become records of their lives, blurring the boundary of narrative forms as the novel dives into geography, mythology, and archeology. Yet, the beating heart of the story remains these four generations of women, all storytellers in their own way. The narrator/mother is writing her own novel about a mother and daughter on a journey; meanwhile, the daughter is documenting their trip through letters and photographs to her grandmother, whose memory is rapidly failing––archiving memories for the one who is losing them. 

The result: a novel that folds time and writing itself. A tripartite novel with three suitcases, a title in three parts, and a fourth layer nestled inside, like the great-grandmother of the stolen relic and the memories the characters in Beginning Middle End are trying to piece together. The story leaves the reader wondering how fractured memories can be preserved and told through fabricated narratives. What is it to live in the middle when memories are fading away?

Valeria Luiselli and I are both Mexican writers, born on the same day of the same year, both living in the United States. Via Zoom, we talked about sounds, migration, tectonic plates, translation, and the power of fiction and narrative to shape children’s imaginations. 



(Aşağıdaki metin orijinal dilindedir. Söyleşinin tamamına kaynak siteden ulaşabilirsiniz.)

Ofelia Montelongo: As I was reading the novel, I kept thinking about how themes of displacement and the mother-daughter relationship have been central to your earlier work. How did your earlier work migrate into the imagination of this novel?

There’s always a moment in a novel when you have to abandon a path because you are already on another. Those abandoned paths are ones that I often pick up again in another book.

Valeria Luiselli: There is a line of continuity in many of my books. Maybe not a line that traverses all of them. I certainly see a very clear line from Los ingrávidos or Faces in the Crowd (2011), through this tiny thing I wrote that very few people have read called Swings of Harlem––a map of swings in Harlem where I started using Polaroid photography for the first time while documenting, in that case, a neighborhood and the swings in the neighborhood. And then, from Swings Of Harlem to Lost Children Archive and, of course, Tell Me How it Ends as well, but that’s a very straightforward, nonfictional testimonial piece.

OM: How are the narrators and main characters different in each story? And different from you as the author? 

VL: The characters are not the same. The narrator has a different profession in each of the books. In Los Ingrávidos she’s a translator, in the Lost Children Archive, she’s a sound documentarist. And in the Beginning Middle End, she’s a fiction writer.

The narrator somehow has grown alongside me. You know, it’s like she’s a kind of presence in my life, as are her children, stepchildren, and half children. It’s sort of this lightly alternate world that communicates. Not so much with mine, but with my curiosities, with my pains, with my desire to understand things a little deeper.

I always end up writing about what I don’t know when I start writing a book, and the process of writing it is a process of me trying to get closer to knowing something. It’s the process of inquiry and research, deep essaying, trying things out, and there are always things left unexplored or not explored to the depth at which I would have liked to explore them. There’s always a moment in a novel when you have to abandon a path because you are already on another. Those abandoned paths are ones that I often pick up again in another book.

OM: One of the narrative forms you use in this book is sound, something you’ve also explored in your previous work. Can you talk about that choice and what drew you to it?

VL: In Lost Children Archive, I started delving deeply into sound. Sound as a medium, and as a space for deeper listening and deeper attention. But I explored it more at a level of fiction and theory. I read about it, I imagined it, I explored on paper, but I didn’t explore it in life. Shortly after, that exploration led me to a much deeper involvement in sound with Echoes from the Borderlands, where a daughter is also present, and I formed a collective with two other collaborators. Together, we’ve been documenting soundscapes in the borderlands for almost six years.

That was a seed that was planted in Lost Children and later bloomed into this project. Similar to Echoes from the Borderlands and Lost Children, I started having a deeper curiosity about observing the natural world and thinking about deserts and borders—not only human-made borders, but deeper, even tectonic borders, and trying to understand natural phenomena. I explore that much further in Beginning Middle End. It also takes place on a border.

OM: What kind of sounds can the reader expect on Beginning Middle End?

Sicily is an island that has belonged to everyone and to no one; no one belongs to it, and everyone belongs. It’s a very bizarre kind of borderland.

VL: There is an entire layer of sound that we recorded on-site in Sicily, and we recorded all the winds mentioned. We recorded underwater soundscapes and currents, beautiful volcanic exhalations––which sound a little like thunder, so I really hope the listeners understand that what they’re listening to is a volcano and not thunder. Strangely, volcanoes and thunder sound very similar.

We recorded fish markets where fishermen are screaming, saying things, and singing about swordfish. We have this entire sonic landscape that we are spreading together with the narrative, and not a single sound is stock sound. All sounds were recorded there. They’re very subtle. They’re more like a sort of Greek chorus, an emotional undercurrent for the novel. That translation work, like going from text to sound, has been such a beautiful experience, and as with everything, there are things lost in translation.

For example, the images are not part of the sound. When you are listening to it, you do not have images, but you have the entire sonic landscape, which is a very embodied way of being in a space, just as images allow you to see and embody a space.

OM: What is the significance of Sicily in the story? And how does it represent a border?

VL: Sicily is the border of Africa and Europe. But it is, first of all, a tectonic border, meaning the tectonic plate of Africa meets the tectonic plates of Europe under Sicily. As a result of the friction between those two tectonic plates, there is volcanic activity in the area, the bizarre winds, and the strange currents.

It’s a geological tectonic border, but it is also a geopolitical tectonic border. Most of the migration that eventually arrives on the European continent makes its first landing in Sicily and its surrounding islands.

Sicily has always been an island where all the cultures of the Mediterranean and, expanding outward even inland areas around the Mediterranean, have met, have clashed, have made wars, have coincided, have co-inhabited. It is an island that has belonged to everyone and to no one; no one belongs to it, and everyone belongs. It’s a very bizarre kind of borderland.

OM: Speaking about borderlands, the theme of migration is part of the story—perhaps not as pronounced as in other books you have written, but still there. The mother and the daughter are migrating somewhere.

VL:  Everyone might have to migrate at some point. It is human history. Be it political violence, environmental catastrophe, or whatever other reason, it has always dictated great diasporas and migrations.

We never know who is next. People in richer nations tend to forget their own past of migration. Italians forget that they had to migrate out of poverty and that they migrated to Cuba and Mexico. My Spanish grandfather migrated to Cuba at age 12 to work as a carpenter.

Years later, he went to Veracruz, then settled in Mexico and worked in a factory. Contemporary Spain and Italy might not remember how much they owe to their people in America and the U.S. We just never know who’s next.

OM: It is interesting to consider that the characters are migrating toward their memories. The narrator talks about the three parts, beginning, middle, and end, but there is also a fourth part, the great-grandmother Nanna. The mother and daughter are looking to recover her memories. Memories that are no longer there. It is like an imaginary border of memories. Can you talk a bit more about the stories that are lost due to migration?  

VL: It is only through contact with the other, in this case, someone from the past, that we come to resignify and better understand our present. Coming into contact with the past—the past of a family—is an antidote to cultural amnesia.

Stories of migration have to be told and talked about to understand one’s own origins, but also the deeper past. The mythological past that informed our conception of the world, how we organize a sense of time, our narrative of catastrophes, all of that is deeply coded in the ancients.

It’s also like passing the story on to the next generation, which I think is very important not only in literature but in everyday life. What instruments do we give the next generation so they can retell and reimagine the story?

OM: The narrator is also a fiction writer who explores the possibility of writing about a mother-daughter journey, and she wonders whether, in interviews, she would be asked whether this is autofiction or based on real events. I love the layers of fiction intertwined in these possibilities, which might make others ask you, the author Valeria, if Beginning Middle End is based on a real story. I love that we will never know. 

We all have a right to imagine. We should exercise it freely.

VL: Not only that, but it doesn’t really matter, I mean, I understand human curiosity, we all have it. We all want to know what happened—todos somos chismosos—it’s part of the delight of human conversation. In terms of trying to understand a work of literature better, it really doesn’t help us. It’s a dead-end street, because there’s no yes or no answer.

Did this actually happen? Yes. So, what?

Did this actually happen? No. Okay. So does it really shine light on a piece of work? I really don’t think so.

It’s a kind of non-consequential conversation. If it’s real or not, who cares? I mean, we want to know, but really, it doesn’t matter.

OM: It’s also an invitation to the reader to create their own fiction, and wonder, “Do they return the mosaic? What happens next?”

VL: I think we all have a right to imagine. We should exercise it freely. I like to leave doors open for that in my work, not only for readers to be a very active part of the construction of a story, but even for my future self.

First of all, because I don’t know how to be in the world if I’m not writing actively. I do very badly in the real world if I’m not also in the process of constructing another reality. I have learned to trick myself into leaving, in each book that I open, the door for the next. An invitation for the next.

OM: Let’s talk about translation. Your work has been translated into various languages, and you have also translated at least one of your books. How was the translation process for this book?

VL: This is the first book I [wrote] where I wouldn’t even use the term translation. I wrote it in both languages, period. I didn’t translate from one to the other. I just wrote it in those languages. I had previously done something like that with Tell Me How It Ends, but it was different because I first wrote a version in English and then translated it. What English there was, I translated into Spanish, but what really happened was that I wrote a lot more in Spanish than I originally did in English. That became the essay of Los niños perdidos, and then that was re-translated [into English], partly by the translator Lizzie Davis. That book went through several stages and layers of writing in one language, translating, then re-translating, and it became a book thanks to that back and forth. 

In this case, I simply wrote both of them in both. The chronology of it is messy; it’s not quite retellable. Not linear. Which also means it’s not a translation. I wrote it in both languages. 

The post Migration Touches Every Life appeared first on Electric Literature.

title: 3 Debut Authors Discuss How to Live in the Hypothetical
desc: For the spring edition of our debut craft series, three debut authors—Alexa Yasemin Brahme, Sonia Feldman, and Vincent Yu—discuss in detail their journeys through writing about imaginary lives. One ma...
content:
For the spring edition of our debut craft series, three debut authors—Alexa Yasemin Brahme, Sonia Feldman, and Vincent Yu—discuss in detail their journeys through writing about imaginary lives. One may argue that all fiction is rooted in imaginary lives, but these novels especially feel centered around the stakes of these imaginary lives as the protagonists confront, examine, wonder, and muse upon each of their choice’s ramifications on the rest of their years. From the gritty-and-glamorous art scene of Manhattan to the humid teenage June of northeastern Ohio to a suburban, emergency-laden town in Massachusetts, these three novels feature forks in the road and irreversible decisions that fall like dominoes upon characters and their next chapters. 

“It was strange to see John in the studio, completely at a loss as to how to move his body, unsure of how to orient himself toward art.” So begins Good News by Alexa Yasemin Brahme, a novel centered on Maggie, a Turkish-American MFA student finalizing her evocative thesis painting of “feminine suffering” while competing with her brother’s girlfriend, who has given herself the moniker of “the Artist.” Set in the contemporary New York art scene, the novel follows Maggie as she tries to orient herself within a branching future. Through gallery openings, social climbing parties, doubts about her boyfriend, and the return of an enigmatic ex, Maggie is forced to decide which life or alternate life she’ll end up choosing. In this world, a vertical brushstroke can change the entire canvas, and one phone call can upend everything she’s built. Good News invites it all, plus the chaos, pleasure, and temptation of being young—that is, of creating worlds that leak out of our heads. 

“Growing up, I had two best friends—Margaret, whom I had known my whole life, and Eleanor, with whom I was in love, though for years I had no reason to tell my feelings for one apart from my feelings for the other.” In Girl’s Girl by Sonia Feldman—set in that long summer between freshman and sophomore year of high school—Mina is caught in a web of desire, both platonic and erotic. It is a novel about living in suburban Ohio and creating those “capital E Experiences” that stay with you long after graduation. Reading it, I could almost smell the chlorine of untouched pools and that sticky perfume of bug spray sweating off skin at the end of the night. The messiness of the Midwest summer and unrequited love and dazzling adolescent confessions run rampant in this debut. 

 



(Aşağıdaki metin orijinal dilindedir. Söyleşinin tamamına kaynak siteden ulaşabilirsiniz.)

“Beckitt’s emergency began on a calm spring morning: an expansive chill in the air; the sun soaring over rangy, adolescent clouds; miles of rolling green mowed into submission, flanked by grand columns of oak and maple, through which the wind shivered.” When a ballistic missile alert threatens the town of Beckitt on a mundane morning, the town and its cast of characters are confronted with that most human decision: fight-or-flight. But when the second alert comes in, claiming that the first was a false alarm, the real decisions become clear. Where does one go from here? What did each person choose to save or leave behind? And how will these ramifications infiltrate the rest of their lives and those surrounding them? Seek Immediate Shelter by Vincent Yu explores the question of “what if” at its zenith. The novel follows five different characters and moves through each of their perspectives when the alert was sent, and then the aftermath, which for some may prove to be an even more daunting emergency than that initial missile threat. 

Brahme, Feldman, and Yu corresponded with me on the significance of perspective in their novels, the spark that ignited and transformed their hypothetical questions into fiction, and the advice they would impart to anyone becoming a debut novelist. 

Kyla D Walker: Did you know right away that the book would be from Maggie’s third-person limited POV, or did you consider a first-person POV as well? What ultimately led you to choose third-person narration, and how did this change the novel’s approach?

Alexa Yasemin Brahme: First person is an intimidating point of view—“I” can be very powerful. First person felt immediate, intimate, and had a sure-footedness that wasn’t quite right for Maggie. The first person feels to me like certainty. We readers are getting the account straight from the source, and when that source is unreliable, like I think Maggie would be, the first person feels like a slight of hand a character is performing against the reader. What’s presented as fact is actually distorted. I wanted there to be a little distance between the reader and Maggie so she couldn’t hide from their gaze. Maggie can’t present her take on the situation because the reader can see multiple sides at once. While Maggie can trick herself into believing one version of the story, she can’t trick the reader. 

That said, when I was drafting and editing the book, if I got stuck in certain scenes wondering what Maggie would say or do, I would write them in first person to see if there was anything Maggie could reveal to me about herself. If it proved to be useful, I’d take what I’d written and massage it into a third-person version for the final draft. 

First person is an intimidating point of view—’I’ can be very powerful.

KDW: I love Maggie’s thesis painting and all it represents, and I’m so curious about its conception. Did the painting’s concept—the image of multiple women in mundane settings yet extreme pain—come before the novel, or did it arise through the novel’s writing and Maggie’s character?

AYB: The painting was challenging for me to conceive of while I was writing the book. Turns out, not being a visual artist is a huge impairment to writing about visual art. When I started working on the novel, I had no idea what the painting would depict. I knew I wanted the subject of the work to be about women and their particular plight in this world. And it wasn’t crucial, at least to me, that the painting be perfectly visible throughout the book. My main concerns were the feelings surrounding the art. At times, the painting feels bleak and depressing, and later in the book, Maggie realizes its greater meaning is deeper than just “Women Suffer.” 

Strangely, writing the painting felt like a process Maggie and I were constructing together. It feels like we figured it out, which makes me sound absolutely insane. 


KDW: Which part of the writing process required much more time and energy than you initially expected? And which was your favorite part of the process?

AYB: I couldn’t anticipate how any part of the writing process was going to go, which was challenging, and unfortunately seems to be emerging as a pattern. Sometimes a scene would rush by while I was writing, and then there would be a month of agony when I didn’t know what was going to happen next. It seemed there was nothing I could force that would speed up the agony. In these waiting periods, I’d watch a lot of movies, go to museums, read books, listen to music, all in hopes that I might feel something new or think a new thought. Sometimes it worked, and sometimes it didn’t. The key was trying not to feel too depressed when it didn’t work, and to just keep showing up until eventually something showed up on the page with me. 

The most fun part of the process is when these horrible periods end because of a single thought that flashes in my mind and feels like it solves all my problems. Likely it solves one or two, but after suffering, anything feels like a rushing wave of relief. Then when things click into place after that rough patch and the writing is moving again, my memory is short enough to forget ever having suffered in the first place. 


KDW: And finally, what advice would you now give to anyone currently working on a debut novel? 

AYB: My advice to anyone working on anything creative is to try to stay connected to yourself. It is so tempting to share a scene with someone, an early sketch of something, and wait for them to tell you how good it is. But more often than not that experience isn’t as rewarding as you think it’s going to be. Maybe someone says it’s amazing, and you don’t believe them. Or worse, maybe you do believe them and it’s, tragically, not yet amazing. Someone may not understand what you’re doing, which isn’t their fault but can be absolutely crushing. Someone may be jealous and dismissive, which can discourage you from continuing on.

Whatever you’re making, it’s a delicate thing for a longer time than I ever realized. I was glad when I was writing my debut, that I protected it from outside forces until it (and I) had enough body and heft to withstand other people’s reactions. People could say whatever they wanted about the work, and I had spent enough time with it, built a relationship with it, that I knew if their comments were brilliant critiques I had to incorporate, or well-meaning remarks that had no bearing on what the book would become. That way, I’ll say most of the time, I didn’t take things personally. I was in conversation with the work, other people were saying things, and sometimes those things were right, and sometimes they weren’t. It didn’t always have to be so painful. 

KDW: When was the moment you felt ready to begin writing Girl’s Girl? And what was that initial spark—maybe a specific sentence, scene, or character’s voice—that kicked off the writing of the novel?

I had to ask myself: Would you prefer to write a bad book or to write no book?

Sonia Feldman: I wrote poetry for years before I started writing fiction, and I entered this book the way I usually enter a poem—with a sense of emotional atmosphere. I knew that the protagonist, Mina, was in a very particular, difficult to express mood. My poetry also almost always has weather, temperature, or a time of year. I think I need this kind of information in order to feel oriented. So I also knew from the very start that Mina’s mood had to take place in the summer. It was a summer kind of feeling. From there, I began the long and slow process of asking why Mina felt that way and trying to turn her mood from something I could feel into something I could help someone else feel.

KDW: Did you know right away that the book would be told in first person? Did you consider third person or a shifting POV to capture Eleanor and Margaret’s interior monologues as well? 

SF: I spent several years trying to write Girl’s Girl in the third person and basically banging my head against the wall. I really wanted to write in the third person because I grew up loving 18th century British literature and Jane Austen, especially. Also, I was afraid to write in the first person. But I couldn’t figure out who that third person voice telling the story was. She wasn’t me, but she also wasn’t a character defined by the book. I would try to describe Mina, Margaret, and Eleanor in an omniscient narrator’s voice, and then immediately disagree with my own descriptions. Only once I let myself write as Mina did the perspective of the voice telling the story start to make sense. Because then the book no longer had to contain “true” descriptions of the characters. Instead, it merely had to offer Mina’s opinions about herself and the people around her at a given moment in time.

KDW: What did research for Girl’s Girl look like? 

SF: Calling my best friends on the phone and asking them what they fought about with their moms when they were 15. Attending a county fair as an adult. Deep and sustained introspection. Reading girlhood and coming-of-age novels like Dogs of Summer by Andrea Abreu (translated by Julia Sanches), Sweet Days of Discipline by Fleur Jaeggy (translated by Tim Parks) and How Should a Person Be? by Sheila Heti. Reading novels that were tonally quite different from mine but had incredible first person retrospective narrators, like Never Let Me Go by Kazuo Ishiguro, Housekeeping by Marilynne Robinson, and The Emigrants by WG Sebald. Rewatching Sailor Moon. Looking up the lifecycle of nodding thistle. Playing The Sims.

KDW: And finally, what advice would you give to anyone currently working on a debut novel? 

SF: What comes to mind is a kind of crisis that I had during the writing experience. I was incredibly frustrated with the book and my own lack of progress. I’d been trying to write it in the third person for years and had what felt like nothing to show for it. I had no story, no causality, just a bunch of information about people. I had a pile of pages that weren’t in any way a book. This felt horrible.

I suspected that I might be able to make progress if I tried writing in the first person instead. I really didn’t want to do this. I was afraid of what I would produce if I did. I felt like if I wrote the book in the first person, then it wouldn’t be the book I’d been dreaming of because it wouldn’t sound the way I’d been dreaming it would sound. So in effect, I would be letting go of a dream of what the book could be.

Another way of saying this is that I felt like if I wrote the book in the first person—I might be able to actually write it, but—the book would be bad. And so I had to ask myself: Would you prefer to write a bad book or to write no book? Because those were my two options. I had to truly in my heart accept that I’d rather write a bad book that embarrassed me than to write no book at all. I think if you can do that, you can finish your manuscript. And then you can try to make it better.

KDW: The concept of Seek Immediate Shelter and the stories that unravel throughout feel like a thought experiment and a fictional philosophical journey through the different decisions and shocking paths one may take in times of crisis, touching upon the faults of human nature and the complicated expectations and nuanced responses individuals have against a collective/conventional society. How did the idea of the false missile crisis come about, and what led you to follow an eclectic cast of characters rather than a single protagonist?

Vincent Yu: Seek Immediate Shelter began as a question that would not go away: What would I do if I thought I might die at any moment? Writing fiction has always been a means of self-discovery as well as self-expression, and so my instinct, after continuing to be nagged by this hypothetical, was to explore it in a story. When I recalled the 2018 ballistic missile alert sent in error to Hawaii, I realized that a fictionalized version of this event might create the ideal set of conditions under which to investigate the gut reaction of a flawed but believable human being. 

It’s really apt that you use the term “thought experiment” to describe this book—that is precisely the mindset I had when I started writing! The book actually began as a short story with a single character, exploring his response to the alert and its rippling effects. 

Robust experiments, however, often require multiple iterations and control groups in order to capture the full scope of investigation, to take into account the truly surprising results and novel conclusions. And so, after I finished that first story, I realized that I wanted to do more with the idea: I wanted to pressure test an entire battery of characters with an equivalent variety of behaviors. That was how the book really came into being.

KDW: With so many varied occupations represented—from violinists to PR executives—what did the research process for this novel look like?

Every form of discovery begins as a kind of disturbance.

VY: The research involved in writing this book was fairly light, in large part because I was a competitive pianist and violinist growing up, and because my first career was in public relations! I wanted very much to write what I knew—that way I could focus a bit more on creating empathetic and convincing psychologies for people who experienced things with which I was unfamiliar: parenthood, substance abuse, false missile alerts (!), and such. 

The most research-heavy chapter was the sixth, in which I follow the character who worked at the Emergency Management Agency and actually sent out the false alert. This required investigation into the bureaucratic processes that are actually involved in sending out such notifications. It also gave me tremendous, terrifying insight into how fallible these kinds of systems are, and how quickly a single offhand decision can yield a runaway reaction.

There were also moments in which research popped up out of necessity. For example, when I needed to determine the best way to acquire a dead person’s DNA for a paternity test, or to understand various bluegrass violin techniques, or to clarify the human pupil’s reaction to opioid use, among others. Falling down these little rabbit holes and emerging with greater knowledge, however random it may be, is one of the greatest pleasures of writing fiction. 

KDW: Did you write Seek Immediate Shelter with an outline or a specific order for each character’s chapter in mind?

VY: Not really. The idea of a literary experiment really took hold of me from the very beginning, which led to a large amount of trial and error in my writing process. I let each character make his or her own decisions, and then tried to gauge as honestly as possible if their behaviors seemed believably human. There were a lot of false starts and many branching plot points that I pursued and ultimately pruned. 

The whole process was a bit like mapping out a completely dark room. I started in the middle, without knowing the shape of the space I was in or its contours or objects. I had no choice, really, but to move and feel my way around. I bumped into many things, but I think every form of discovery begins as a kind of disturbance. After a while I began to feel more confident in my explorations.

The real light switch, however, was my editor, Caroline Bleeke. Her guidance and vision for the manuscript was completely illuminating. Once she and I started working together, I knew exactly how to order the stories and unite the characters into a cohesive whole. 

Matthew Salesses, author of “Disappear Doppelgänger Disappear,” recommends stories about multiple selves

KDW: How did the backdrop of Beckitt help sculpt the story or shift the style of prose, if at all? And is the town’s name a direct allusion to a certain canonical existentialist absurdist writer? 

VY: Ha! There was a little bit of intentionality in my choice of the town name, but certainly not enough to put the work in any meaningful dialogue with that of Beckett’s. All I really wanted was to invoke a sense of strangeness even in the everyday. Beckitt was actually based on my own hometown of Longmeadow, which is also located in the Pioneer Valley of Western Massachusetts.

After I decided to tell the story through multiple characters, I realized that setting the entire thing in a single community would allow me to believably intertwine their lives and to explore the particular drama that occurs in small, tight-knit communities. 

Many people (including some of the characters in the book) assume that towns like Beckitt are perennially quiet and unchanging. One of my goals in sending a false missile alert to its residents was to create enough of an emotional disturbance to reveal the richness of all the lives within it, the vast interiorities of every single resident, living and dead.

title: Finding Your Voice as a Woman Writer Raised on Books by Men
desc: Julie Buntin and I first met when Electric Literature shared an office with Catapult in the mid-2010s. She was a book editor and the director of Catapult’s beloved educational program; I had recently ...
content:
Julie Buntin and I first met when Electric Literature shared an office with Catapult in the mid-2010s. She was a book editor and the director of Catapult’s beloved educational program; I had recently become Electric Literature’s Executive Director. I was an aspiring writer with a few short stories; Julie was about to publish her debut novel, Marlena, to critical and commercial acclaim. We hit it off as two hard-working, mostly type-A people with the same cynical sense of humor that protects over-eager emotions, and began trading work after we both left the city. Julie to Ann Arbor where she was teaching at the University of Michigan and writing her sophomore novel, Famous Men; me to upstate New York where I was working on my debut novel, Slush, which will be published next summer. Julie is my most trusted reader. I have long felt like I can say anything to her; that nothing is too strange, or dark, or vulnerable, or naïve. If I am working out a difficult opinion, she can help me articulate it. What better qualities to have in a writing partner?

Famous Men tells the story of Wilhelmina Miles, known as Will, an aspiring poet from the small town of Greening, Michigan. She has long harbored the fantasy that her town’s one success story, the decorated writer Nathanial Fellow, is her father. When she moves to New York and tracks him down at the MFA program where he teaches, that fantasy deforms into a relationship, one that is financial, professional, sexual, and even a little familial.

Famous Men is an entertaining, rich, discomfiting novel that rejects black and white answers to complex questions in favor of subjectivity as its foundational stance. Consent is not a matter of “yes” or “no,” culpability is not an easy verdict, and power is multi-directional.

Reading early drafts of Famous Men, I was struck by how they never quite felt like drafts. Scenes were cut, plot points changed, etc., but the world of the novel and the ideas behind it always felt fully formed. Julie has a charismatic prose style that is flowing yet precise, with a clarity of insight that seems casual but is most certainly hard won. When the galley finally arrived, I thought I would dip in and out to gather questions for this interview. But I couldn’t resist reading straight through for a third time; the novel is that compelling and rewarding.



(Aşağıdaki metin orijinal dilindedir. Söyleşinin tamamına kaynak siteden ulaşabilirsiniz.)

Julie and I spoke over video call, with some follow-up over email. I found myself surprisingly nervous to ask her “serious questions” on the record, after so many casual, private conversations. Initial giggling aside, we settled in, and I was grateful to be able to engage with her not as my friend, but as the author of one of my favorite books of this decade.

Halimah Marcus: Will, long before she ever meets Nathaniel, reads his work at the library. And because they’re from the same small town, it sparks her imagination about what she could be someday. Who were the writers that did that for you when you were that age?

Julie Buntin: I grew up in Hemingway country. I grew up in the Petoskey area of Northern Michigan where the Nick Adams stories on Walloon Lake are set. Hemingway lived in a lot of places, but there’s a lot of regional Hemingway pride where I’m from in a way I took for granted as a young person—that a small town like that might celebrate their literary grandfather out of pride. My husband’s family is from Lorain, Ohio, where Toni Morrison is from, and he went looking for her house once. There was nothing that said Toni Morrison lived there.

Hemingway was a writer I liked and read at a young age because we had his books in our house, The Sun Also Rises, For Whom the Bell Tolls, obviously the stories. I wasn’t necessarily thinking, I want to write like this, but I did have this idea of certain writers as having this cultural impact. I also read a ton of Stephen King, like so much Stephen King.

HM: Will internalizes a lot of lessons from being so obsessed with Nathaniel’s work. There’s this great passage about all the women in Nathaniel’s fiction, and the limits of who they could be and the archetypes they represent. Did you internalize any lessons like that from your reading as a young person?

JB: With this book, I wrestled a lot with questions I still sit with. I remember reading Herzog by Saul Bellow as a teenager and thinking: This is genius. The high/low voice; it’s so funny. How does he do this? This is everything I could ever want to do as a writer. And then having a similar reaction to the Rabbit, Run novels by John Updike, loving them without any ability at that age to question the complicated portrayals of women, which are sometimes really reductive.

In this book, I was thinking a lot about what happens if part of your formative artistic development involves taking in influences that don’t always make space for your full subjectivity as a person. What happens if those are the models you put ahead of everything else? If the first character you identify with in serious literature is like, a middle-aged man? I was thinking about not only how that would affect you as a writer, but how it would affect your sense of what kind of woman you wanted to be or could be.

We’re so permeable to influence when we’re children and adolescents, especially. I see this with my son, who is five—he reads something and suddenly he’s repeating phrases from it, acting like the characters. That’s something I’m endlessly interested in, so that was floating around in my head for sure: How might there be bleeding between what Will reads and what she thinks? How she presents herself to Nathaniel, how she understands how he might see her—all of that is a creation of her imagination, but also created by the texts of his that she’s read.

HM: Later in the book, Will asks Vilma, Nathaniel’s ex and a writer with acclaim and success, if Vilma was ever afraid that her stories weren’t important or literary enough because they were about all the things women thought and felt. I love this moment, because it’s in a book about everything a woman thought and felt. Did you ever have the feeling that this book isn’t important because it is about a woman?

JB: I had that feeling a lot when I was writing my first book [Marlena]. When I started writing it in my MFA, I remember getting a lot of feedback that boiled down to things like, why do we care about what teenage girls are doing? There were obviously other problems with the early drafts, but there was often a question of, is this YA? YA is wonderful—I would love to write it sometime—but that question wasn’t a question. It was a way of saying that the material doesn’t feel high stakes because of what it’s about.

For example, I remember learning about Who Will Run the Frog Hospital [by Lorrie Moore] in grad school, and it being presented as a kind of failed novel, where the girlhood sections were dragging down this more interesting potent story of an adult relationship, and thinking, when I finally read it, girlhood is the point of this book.

HM: One of the culminations of Famous Men happens during the height of the #MeToo movement, when the Harvey Weinstein news is breaking. At the time, pretty much immediately, people started talking about #MeToo novels, even applying the term to novels that were written before—novels that embodied the values of the #MeToo movement, in terms of believing women or the value of consent and autonomy, novels that were expressing often painful stories of sexual violence and abuses of power.

Famous Men engages deeply with those themes. But reading that part of the book, I thought about how this novel is a document of #MeToo and everything that led up to it, even more than a “#MeToo novel.” Because it all started 10 years ago, which makes it practically historical fiction. What’s your relationship with that term today? How do you feel it’s changed over time: in the last 10 years, and while writing this novel?

JB: This book took me many years to write. I started it in the summer of 2019, which I remember as a moment of almost hopefulness. There was some sense of a public reckoning having happened, and of justice or change that was going to be lasting and positive. Maybe I’m just too optimistic in general, but I was like, okay, this is hard but what will come out of it is a slightly better world.

When I started writing in my MFA, I remember getting a lot of feedback that boiled down to, why do we care about what teenage girls are doing?

I finished the book last year. And now we’re in a time when there are even scarier questions to ask: Was any progress real? Has the backlash to #MeToo actually undone the positive things about #MeToo? What was that? Was #MeToo just another version of something that’s happened over and over, and now we’re in a more regressive place? I had children during that time. My son was born in 2021, when I was still kind of hoping for some sort of brighter future. My daughter was born in 2024, and I fear she’ll have less rights and protections than I have.

When #MeToo happened, there was a sense that what was publicly condoned three months ago is no longer okay. Of a real turning point. And I thought, what would it be like to tell this story from the perspective of a character who can’t inhabit that shift because of various things that are happening in her life?

HM: Because she feels implicated.

JB: She feels implicated and she feels stuck. She’s implicated because of the choices she’s made. She’s implicated because of her relationship with this person [Nathaniel], which is financial. She’s financially dependent on him, but she also loves him. I say love, not even in a sexual or romantic way; it’s almost like a friendship by the end of the book.

HM: I love how Will and Nathaniel’s first encounters, at a reading she attends and then in his office, set up the dynamics of their future relationship. She acts in surprising ways. He probably acts more predictably, in terms of what we might expect a guy like that to do. At the reading, he’s goes to help her carry chairs, and he touches her leg. She thinks it’s the wrong kind of first touch. In their second meeting, she’s at his office and drops a book, and when she goes to pick it up, she pushes it further under the table, and then ties his shoe. The moment is so surprising to everyone involved, including the reader.

JB: Including her.

HM: The gesture is at once submissive in kind of a sexual way, and also infantilizing to him. The way I read it, when he touches her leg, she’s learning what he expects from her. And then when she ties his shoe, she’s delivering on what he expects. She’s one step ahead. Where does that kind of intuition come from?

JB: It’s every story she’s internalized and read. She knows Nathaniel’s work really well. She knows the kind of move he might respond to. And when she has that moment with him at the reading, she realizes something about what character she would be to him. Once she knows what character she would be to him, she understands how to get his attention. She’s a character who kind of wants his attention no matter what, even after she realizes that he’s not the person that she thought he was. She has come there for him, or because of a vision of life that his work offered her. It’s parasocial. It’s a fantasy. But once she’s there, she is intoxicated by this world that she sees at this reading. Moving to New York alone at a young age can make anybody kind of bananas. She doesn’t have anyone. She doesn’t have any friends. She’s on her own.

So the step that is crucial to that moment is knowing his work as well as she does, and having this instinct about what Nathaniel might respond to. This is a way of getting at some of these questions about the male gaze and how the pressure of it over the course of a lifetime can make you act in ways that feel as if they are not coming from your true, essential self. Or that you’re being steered by something outside of you, which is an experience I certainly felt as a young woman. Who am I doing this for? What norm am I trying to satisfy with this? Who am I trying to satisfy?

HM: From the first chapter, Will breaks one of Nathaniel’s rules, which is: If you need the past to tell a story, you’re telling the wrong story. The book begins in her small town of Greening and deals a lot with the way she experiences the male gaze. She gets negative attention from the boys in her school because she has big boobs, and she feels like her mother’s boyfriend is always watching her. I wonder if there’s actually something feminist about including the past in this way.

I’m interested in passivity in fiction, and passivity in women.

JB: I hope that that is how it’s read. You might get through this whole book and be like, Will makes bad decisions, she’s an imperfect character in all of these ways, she doesn’t learn anything, and she doesn’t grow. She compromises left and right; what kind of vision of feminism is this? Is this feminist? You could absolutely have that reaction. The way Will tells her story, and the choices she makes about when to break the rules she has been taught are givens, is an act of agency. A declaration of, “I no longer adhere to this narrative that trapped me for so long” and “I will not tell it the way he would teach me to.” A lot of those choices were happening on a structural level, like when and where to start the story, or to cut.

HM: Some readers might be frustrated with Will for her perceived passivity. There’s so much that happens with Nathaniel that she feels is a foregone conclusion, probably because she’s anticipating his expectations. She’s dictating her own fate while also feeling like it’s pre-written. How is that a strength for her and how is it a liability?

JB: We all have these things as writers that creep in, book to book or project to project. I’m interested in passivity in fiction, and passivity in women. One true thing about how I have experienced the world that I’ve not always been able to find in literature is: What does it mean to be socialized in every way to make things easier for other people, to be helpful, to be accommodating of everyone at the expense of yourself, to not cause a ruckus? I was raised in that mold, and so much of my experience of coming of age has been about dealing with those impulses in myself in every context and trying to figure out when they serve me and when they don’t.

Will is incredibly self-determined and she’s not passive at all until she gets stuck in a system where the power is so out of whack that she can’t get it back. She gets in over her head when she’s really young and then she’s swept up in this wave and she’s really stuck. There’s this feeling of time running away from her and “how did I get here?” and “this thing has its own velocity and I’m trapped in it,” which was a way of writing about passivity, and trying to write realistically about those times where you have more self-awareness about what’s going on then you have ability to change it.

HM: Or the will to change it.

JB: I was interested in there being a kind of weird aggressive agency in not acknowledging the truth, in lying to yourself a lot and really hard, and in the ways that you have to lie to yourself if you are opting into certain kinds of relationships that harm yourself or others. A certain amount of self-deception becomes a matter of course, in those contexts.

HM: The violence in Famous Men is very grayed or obscured or sometimes blacked-out, forgotten or confusing to the person who experienced it. The violence in the book that Will writes, the novel within the novel, is very literalized.

JB: That was a really deliberate, conscious choice. You’re not always awake to this in the drafting of a book, but it became more evident to me as I wrote. Especially after I had a first draft. [I wanted to explore] the kinds of violence that are in some way muffled, that might be especially hard for a young woman to define. I have a very clear interpretation of the things that happen to Will as a girl, and where they fall on the violation scale. But Will doesn’t, because of the ways that she’s been raised and the context in which these things happened, and the failure of certain frameworks to protect her, even within her own family.

I was thinking there about what we demand of a victim, or what we need women’s stories to look like in order to feel satisfied that they truly have experienced harm.

Nathaniel gives Will the advice to write something from her life that she can’t stop thinking about. But when she does that, fictionalizing this murky experience she had as a teenager, he tells her to escalate it. I was thinking there about what we demand of a victim, or what we need women’s stories to look like in order to feel satisfied that they truly have experienced harm. We want to know what exactly happened. We need them to look a certain way. I remember taking a cab home from the airport around the time of the Kavanaugh hearings, and the driver brought it up and kept asking, “But how did she get to the second floor?” It was awful.

And why is that? What is unsatisfying about the mess and the confusion and the murk and the ways that all of those things can have years of fallout, and complicated intersections with other kinds of harm that happen later?

HM: Nathaniel reads every draft of Will’s book, he gives her notes, he pushes her towards a bigger plot, essentially leading Will away from herself. But she calls him a good teacher, directly and in various ways throughout. In your opinion, is Nathaniel a good teacher?

JB: I think he is in some ways. You can’t spend six years writing a character and not develop some sympathy. I was inhabiting Will’s point of view, but I have a sense of him outside of that point of view too. I see him as a teacher who is not in his prime anymore. He’s tired, he’s teaching the same shit he’s always taught, he’s not doing anything new in class, he’s regurgitating old lessons. But even his autopilot has moments of profundity that a young writer might be able to latch onto in a way that would be instructive or useful. I do think of him as someone who is interested in his students for personal reasons, but he’s also interested in in their work; at least when it aligns with his taste. That’s the complicated thing about these charismatic teacher figures; sometimes good teachers are good teachers for certain students or for certain kinds of work, or they are good teacher for a minute and then terrible after that, or the longing for their approval outshines any other aspect of what you may or may not learn from them.

HM: As a fiction writer, why did you make the characters poets first?

Mentorship in these books teeter between nurturing and manipulative

JB: There’s something really pure and beautiful to me about poetry. The stakes are incredibly high on a human scale and incredibly low in other ways. There was something about that scale that was really interesting.

Poetry was the first art form I really loved, which is probably in part what this book is talking to. Louise Glück, Elizabeth Bishop, specifically that Elizabeth Bishop poem “In the Waiting Room,” where she has that line where she’s like, why should I be myself? [“Why should I be my aunt, or me, or anyone?”] I remember reading that as a teenager and thinking, this is the ultimate question that one could spend all of life pursuing.
